title: Transistorless cross-point capacitors: two line masks per stacked tier
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: replace the access MOSFET with a two-terminal wide-gap punch-through selector (AlN/SiC heterojunction) whose barrier keeps hot leakage tiny, giving a 4F2 one-selector-one-capacitor cross-point that needs only two line/space masks per tier and stacks monolithically.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 4F2 per tier and ~2 masks per tier vs ~25; cost per bit could fall several-fold if the selector holds fA-class leakage at 125 C.

title: Solid-source diffusion and laser melt anneal replace ion implanters
idea: Revive pre-1975 diffusion doping: spin-on or ALD dopant glasses (B, P, As oxides) patterned by the existing masks are driven in by nanosecond green-laser melt anneal, giving abrupt shallow junctions without ion implanters, argon-purged beamlines or xenon flash lamps. Conformal dopant films also dope 3D sidewalls that tilted implants cannot reach.
why: Capital and the constraint: replaces ~10-15 implanters per DRAM line (~$5-10M each) and flash annealers with spin/ALD tools; conformal sidewall doping helps 3D DRAM (Fact 2). Risks are dose control and junction-leakage tails.

title: Tree-ring shells: coaxial gain cell in every tier-hole crossing
idea: Etch one array of vertical holes through a 100-layer wordline/oxide stack, then grow concentric shells like annual rings: an outer IGZO write-channel ring, a metal storage ring cut into per-tier segments by a selective recess, and an inner read-channel 'heartwood' that the storage ring gates. Each hole-tier crossing becomes a capacitorless 2T0C cell.
why: One hole litho and etch serves all tiers, as in 3D NAND; at ~100 nm hole pitch and 100 tiers that is ~100 nm2 per bit, ~8-10x planar DRAM bits/mm2 at roughly flat wafer cost, with no capacitor (facts 1, 2).

title: Halve EUV dose by designing arrays to absorb stochastic defects
idea: Ideal: EUV throughput doubles for free. Closest: expose array layers at ~30 mJ/cm2 instead of ~60, accepting more stochastic micro-bridges and missing contacts, and absorb them with column/row spares, per-sub-array ECC and a repair map designed in from day one.
why: Fact 4: EUV is the bottleneck tool; ~1.6-1.8x scanner throughput means fewer $150M+ scanners per 10k wafer starts.

title: Spatial ALD carousel boosts dielectric deposition throughput tenfold
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace pulse/purge temporal ALD with wafers rotating under gas-curtain-separated precursor and oxidant zones, so every revolution is one ALD cycle; ZrO2/Al2O3 capacitor dielectrics and liners deposit ~10x faster near atmospheric pressure.
why: ALD is a large share of capacitor and 3D-module tool count; ~5-10x wafers/hour per tool cuts ALD capex and footprint proportionally (throughput, capital).

title: Backside flood exposure through a transparent carrier
idea: Flip the exposure side: build the array on a thin Si layer bonded to fused-silica/sapphire, then flood-expose resist from the backside so already-made opaque wordlines and bitlines act as the photomask for the next self-aligned layer (contacts, spacers).
why: Removes 1-3 critical masks and their overlay budget per generation; mask cost and scanner time drop, overlay-limited yield loss falls.

title: Substitute zirconia capacitor dielectric with templated rutile titania near k=100
idea: Grow rutile-phase TiO2 (k ~80-120) by ALD at <=400 C on a RuO2 bottom electrode whose lattice templates the rutile phase, with Al doping to block leakage, so the same ~5 fF fits in a hole of AR ~25:1 instead of 70:1.
why: Facts 1 and 4: shallower holes cut HAR etch and ALD time ~3x and remove support-mesh steps (or keep AR and double Cs). Ru is itself a scarce metal and leakage is the risk.

title: Self-grown landing pads by selective epitaxial overgrowth
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: let exposed silicon active tips grow their own landing pads - after bitline spacers form, selective Si:P epitaxy with faceted lateral overgrowth fills each storage-node contact and mushrooms to pad size, stopping at the spacer walls, so no landing-pad lithography is needed.
why: Deletes the landing-pad EUV/SAQP layer (one of 5-7 EUV exposures) and its overlay error; ~10-15% EUV cost cut (fact 4).

title: Single-use bioreactor logic: disposable etch-chamber liner cartridges
idea: Biopharma moved from cleaned stainless tanks to single-use bags; give high-AR etch and CVD chambers robot-swappable disposable liner cartridges (yttria-coated alumina shells) replacing 12-24 h wet-clean maintenance.
why: Capital productivity: etch tools are the largest tool count after litho; a 5-10% uptime gain avoids hundreds of millions in tools per fab and stabilizes chamber seasoning.

title: Eliminate retention-test hours: profile weak cells silently inside refresh
idea: Skip the long hot pause and retention tests on ATE; the die uses part of each JEDEC tRFC window to read-compare sample rows at stretched intervals, learns which rows sit in the leakage tail and refreshes them more often internally. The host still issues standard REF commands.
why: Facts 3 and 4: retention screening is among the longest ATE steps; moving it into the field cuts test time ~20-30% and keeps weak-cell dies instead of repairing or scrapping them.

title: CVD-grown carbon-nanotube forests as high-area storage-node electrodes
idea: Box: MIM-on-CNT charge x planar access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x catalytic CVD of vertically aligned CNT bundles from lift-off-patterned Fe/Al2O3 dots on each storage pad. ALD Al2O3/HfO2 and TiN then wrap the forest, whose ~100x surface area per footprint gives fF-scale capacitance from small pads without etching holes.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) by bottom-up growth with a tube furnace and ALD; risk is forest density on sub-100 nm pads, ~600 C growth temperature and ALD nucleation on CNT walls.

title: Never dice: wafer-scale DRAM sold as one memory slab
idea: Inverts 'memory is sold as small diced dies'. Stitch reticles across a full 300 mm wafer, route around dead reticle fields with a wafer-level mesh of fuse-configured links, skip dicing, packaging and per-die test, and ship the whole wafer as a rack CXL memory slab (~3 TB) with optical edge I/O.
why: Eliminates scribe/kerf (~5-8% area), packaging, per-die test and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6); back-end cost per bit -20-30% for pooled capacity tiers.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM panels for rack memory pools
idea: Worse: dice, package and test thousands of dies, each losing scribe and edge area. Flip: keep the whole wafer as one memory, with reticle-stitched interconnect and die/row-level redundancy routing. Mount it directly in a rack memory appliance behind a wafer-level CXL fabric.
why: Packaging, test and scribe are ~15-25% of cost; redundancy turns defects into lost capacity, not scrap; ~20% lower $/GB for pooled memory.

title: Child asks why break the cookie: wafer-scale DRAM, no dicing
idea: A child asks why you bake one big cookie and then break it into crumbs. Keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory: redundant tiles with an on-wafer mesh that maps out bad tiles at test, wafer-level power planes and edge optical I/O, giving a ~1-2 TB rack memory slab per wafer.
why: Eliminates dicing, per-die packaging, per-die test handling and per-die I/O duplication (~10-20% of cost), with yield handled by redundancy instead of scrap. Risks: power delivery and heat across 70,000 mm2, and serviceability.

title: Universal array-tile consortium: one shared mask set across vendors
idea: Box: business axis set to shared mask and process. U.S. and allied fabs standardize a 1T1C array tile (cell pitch, sub-array size, BL/WL interface) whose ~20 array masks and process module are developed once and licensed per wafer, so new entrants and foundries only design periphery.
why: Capital and time to enter (U.S. ~1-2% share): removes ~$50-100M of mask and module development and ~2-3 years per entrant; risk is IP and competitive reluctance.

title: Split-fab DRAM with U.S. capacitor-and-BEOL completion of imported arrays
idea: Extreme user: defense 'trusted foundry' programs that already split fabrication. Import transistor-level array wafers from allied fabs, then complete the capacitor, metallization, test and packaging in a U.S. back-half fab costing ~1/4 of a full fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability: domestic value-add and trust for ~25% of the capital and about 2 years to build.

title: Heat-vanishing polymer capacitor mold eliminates the support lattice
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap sacrificial polymers (thermally decomposable polycarbonate/polynorbornene) with the capacitor mold. Holes are etched in the polymer and low-temperature PEALD electrodes are formed, then the mold is removed by dry burnout rather than an HF wet strip, so no capillary forces topple the pillars.
why: Wet-strip capillary leaning is why 1-3 SiN support lattices are needed. Dropping them removes ~2 masks and ~12 steps and allows AR beyond 75 (facts 1, 4).

title: Eliminate the access transistor: threshold-selector-gated capacitors in BEOL crossbars
idea: Put a two-terminal threshold switch (an ovonic or NbOx selector tuned for femtoamp-class off-current) in series with a MIM capacitor at each wordline/bitline crossing, forming a 1S1C 4F2 cell built entirely in back-end layers and stacked 8+ high.
why: Removes the whole front-end access-transistor module (most critical masks) and stacks with one mask pair per tier; cost per bit could drop 2-3x if selector leakage reaches ~1 fA.

title: Short segmented bitlines with local sense let 1.5 fF capacitors suffice
idea: Box: shallow capacitor charge (~1.5 fF) x standard access x hierarchical local sense amp every 32 cells placed under the array x 2D x Si x capacitor AR ~20. Cutting bitline length from 512-1024 cells to 32 lowers bitline capacitance ~20x, preserving the transfer ratio with a capacitor one third the size, so the capacitor module becomes a shallow single-etch step.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) traded on the sensing axis: AR 70 to 20 removes the highest-capex module and cuts BL CV2 energy ~10x; extra sense amps hide under the array.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching digs 200:1 capacitor holes in a bath
idea: Replace plasma etch with catalytic wet etch: a patterned Pt mesh sinks into a sacrificial silicon mold in HF/H2O2 over minutes, carving vertical holes >200:1 that are then lined with capacitor films and the mold removed with the catalyst.
why: Breaks the AR wall (Fact 1) with a wet bench costing ~1% of a high-AR etcher; domestic chemicals and tooling.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.
why: Meets 100x: tiers are just thin depositions, writes are fast direct tunneling (~10s of ns), retention minutes to hours; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: 3x cell redundancy, calibration time, variability.

title: NbO2 Mott threshold switch replaces the access transistor in BEOL crosspoint
idea: Effect: insulator-metal (Mott/Peierls) transition. An NbO2 two-terminal selector in series with a MIM capacitor is stacked in crosspoint arrays above logic at 2 masks per layer; a sub-threshold hold bias limits leakage and refresh runs in bursts.
why: Capital: no front-end transistor per bit, 4F2 per layer, and 8 layers on cheap BEOL tools. Honest trade: Mott selector off-current is far above 13 fA, so retention is us-ms and this fits a cache or buffer tier.

title: Single-mask vertical thyristor pillars cut from blanket p-n-p-n epitaxy
idea: Ideal: a cell patterned by one exposure. Closest: grow a blanket p-n-p-n Si/SiGe epitaxial stack, cut it into 4F2 pillars with one DSA-assisted hole pattern, and form a self-aligned spacer gate on the p-base; the regenerative thyristor latch stores the bit with no capacitor.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: deletes the capacitor module (~25% of DRAM steps), 4F2 instead of 6F2, ~1 critical array mask; uA read currents simplify sensing.

title: Selector-only chalcogenide crosspoint decks at two masks per layer
idea: Ideal: a cell that is just a wire crossing. Closest: one amorphous chalcogenide threshold-switch layer at each crosspoint whose threshold voltage is set by write polarity (selector-only memory); each deck needs two DUV line masks, decks stack 4-8 high over CMOS, with no capacitor and no transistor per cell.
why: Facts 1, 4, 7: 4F2 per deck with DUV-only patterning and periphery under the array; endurance must reach 10^12+ for DRAM duty, an honest risk.

title: Self-amplifying floating-base bipolar cell needs no sense amplifiers
idea: Ideal: a cell loud enough that the periphery disappears. Closest: a vertical npn whose floating p-base stores holes; on read, the stored charge switches on bipolar gain (beta ~50-100) for uA-level bitline current, so simple inverter sensing replaces pitch-matched differential sense amps, with no capacitor anywhere.
why: Fact 7 and Fact 4: periphery is ~49% of the die; relaxed sense-amp pitch rules shrink it and let it move to a cheaper process; reads need no charge sharing.

title: All-dry, water-lean flow enabled once capacitor dip-out vanishes
idea: Ideal: a memory fab with no ultrapure water. Closest: with no capacitor mold to wet-strip (the HF dip-out and supercritical drying that dominate DRAM wet work), run the capacitorless cell flow on vapor-HF, remote-plasma and cryogenic-aerosol cleans with gas recycling, keeping UPW only for CMP.
why: Resources (water, energy) and capex: UPW plants and wet benches are ~$1B per fab; ~50-70% less UPW opens arid U.S. sites.

title: Laser-crystallized silicon tiers stack refresh-free SRAM toward DRAM density
idea: Ideal: a static, refresh-free cell at DRAM density. Closest: monolithically stack 6-8 tiers of thin single-grain Si, crystallized by pulsed-laser melting of amorphous Si at <450 C wafer temperature, with n and p halves of each SRAM cell on alternate tiers, so bits per footprint multiply with no capacitor and DUV-friendly 28 nm rules.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: no capacitor, no refresh, standard logic tools plus laser anneal; honestly still ~4-8x below DRAM per area today, so the target is cache and buffer tiers.

title: ELTRAN porous-silicon layer transfer reuses seed wafers twentyfold
idea: Revive Canon's 1990s ELTRAN: anodize a CZ seed wafer into a double porous-silicon layer, grow 1-5 um device-grade epitaxial silicon on it in hydrogen with SiHCl3, bond it to a recycled handle with a thin conductive bond, split at the porous layer by water jet, then re-polish and reuse the seed 10-20 times. DRAM front-end steps run in the low-oxygen epi layer.
why: Scarce resources and the constraint: cuts argon-ambient CZ ingot pulling and Spruce Pine quartz crucible use per DRAM wafer by ~10-20x; low-oxygen epi can also tighten the retention tail (Fact 3). Epi reactors run on hydrogen.

title: Gravure-printed redox molecules as storage capacitors
idea: Magnify charge per area by printing a monolayer of porphyrin or ferrocene redox molecules; each molecule stores discrete electrons faradaically, so a planar printed cell stores what a 70:1 pillar does.
why: Capacitor charge wall: about 10x charge density per footprint, which removes high-AR capacitor etch from the process.

title: Reverse logistics: remanufacture retired server DRAM
idea: Reverse the supply flow: build industrial lines that harvest DRAM packages from decommissioned servers, re-ball them, run a burn-in and binning test, and re-module them into certified 'second-life' DIMMs for less demanding tiers.
why: Adds supply with ~1% of fab capex per bit; hyperscalers retire many exabytes-years of working DRAM every year.

title: Film-thickness-defined vertical gain cells need only immersion lithography
idea: Ideal: every critical dimension set by deposition, none by light. Closest: vertical write-over-read transistors in one pillar whose channel lengths equal deposited spacer thicknesses and gate lengths equal ALD metal thicknesses; only pillar placement uses 193i at ~40 nm half pitch, giving a ~4F2 capacitorless 2T gain cell.
why: Fact 4: zero EUV layers and angstrom-level CD control from ALD; with no capacitor the cell is ~300 nm tall instead of ~1.5 um, so fewer deep etches.

title: Fluidic self-assembly of known-good DRAM micro-tiles onto wafer carriers
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x standard sensing x micro-tile assembly x 300 mm passive-RDL carrier x shape-keyed fluidic self-assembly. Tested 1-4 mm2 DRAM tiles (yield ~99% because tiny) are suspended in liquid and settle into keyed recesses on a carrier with fine-pitch RDL, building large memories with near-100% assembled yield and no pick-and-place.
why: Yield and capital: small-tile yield replaces big-die yield loss so a cheaper, EUV-free, higher-defect process becomes economic; ~1e6 tiles/hour vs ~1e4 for pick-and-place; risk is inter-tile interconnect density.

title: Zn: self-evaporating ZnO scaffold opens 3D-DRAM tier gaps
idea: Stack Si/ZnO tiers, cut the vertical slits, then anneal in hydrogen so ZnO is reduced and the high-vapor-pressure Zn evaporates out through the slits, leaving clean cavities for gate and capacitor fill with no selective wet or radical etch.
why: Fact 2: selective lateral SiGe removal across 26+ tiers is a yield/throughput blocker; a thermal sacrificial removal is fully parallel, batchable and has effectively infinite selectivity. Zn contamination control is the risk.

title: Nanoimprint guide plus block-copolymer multiplication for EUV-free capacitor holes
idea: Combine J-FIL-style nanoimprint, which prints a 4x-relaxed hexagonal guide pattern, with high-chi block-copolymer self-assembly that subdivides each guide cell into a 12 nm-scale honeycomb. The densest DRAM layer, the capacitor holes, then needs no EUV and no SAQP.
why: Takes the capacitor-hole layer off EUV: an NIL tool costs ~$30-40M against ~$200M for EUV, roughly halving litho cost for that layer and easing the single-supplier chokepoint (fact 4).

title: Coulomb-blockade nanocrystal chains as a spin-coated ultra-low-leakage access switch
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A vertical chain of 3-5 sub-2 nm Si nanocrystals with 1 nm SiO2 shells, spin-coated from colloid into a via, forms a multi-tunnel junction whose off state is held by a single-electron charging energy above 10 kT at room temperature; a gate lowers the blockade to write the capacitor.
why: Facts 3 and 4: leakage is set by charging energy rather than dopant precision, and the ~20-mask access-transistor FEOL is replaced by BEOL-stackable cells; claimed 100x smaller leakage tail if dot sizes stay uniform.

title: Prestressed buckled nanobeam stores bits as mechanical states
idea: Ideal: a bit that needs no charge at all. Closest: a 200 nm compressively stressed SiN or amorphous-carbon beam released over a BEOL cavity buckles up or down; side electrodes snap it in ~10 ns (GHz resonance) and a non-contact capacitive sense reads position, so the state is held mechanically with zero leakage and no wear.
why: Facts 3 and 4: no capacitor, no refresh, zero standby power; BEOL-only on any logic wafer with 3-4 DUV masks plus a release step.

title: Pyroelectric domain masters print charge patterns like nanoscale xerography
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A LiTaO3 master is written once by e-beam domain poling; a 10 K heat pulse then raises surface charge only on the patterned domains, which picks up charged 10 nm hardmask nanoparticles electrostatically and transfers them to the wafer. The master is reused millions of times.
why: Fact 4 and masks: an optics-free, contact-light patterning tool under ~$5M for periodic array hardmask layers, with the master written only once.

title: Lava lamp: self-assembled multiferroic nanopillars define bits without lithography
idea: Random stimulus 'lava lamp' (blobs separate by themselves) -> co-deposition of BiFeO3 and CoFe2O4 spontaneously phase-separates into vertical magnetic nanopillars about 20 nm apart in a ferroelectric matrix. Each pillar is a non-volatile bit switched by electric-field strain, and a coarse template guides pillar positions.
why: Removes bit-defining lithography and MTJ etch, and gives voltage-written, attojoule-class switching. Risks: growth temperature and registration require the layer to be grown on a template and then bonded.

title: Bottling-line linear fab: single-wafer flow without FOUP queues
idea: Borrow the beverage bottling line: arrange process modules along a linear inert-gas track balanced to one takt time, so each wafer flows step to step singly with no FOUP batching, stockers or overhead hoists; slow modules are duplicated in parallel lanes as in line balancing.
why: Throughput and working capital: cycle time ~60-90 days toward ~10-15 days, WIP inventory down ~5x, AMHS/stocker capex removed, faster yield learning; claim 10-20% capital-productivity gain.

title: MicroLED-style mass transfer of 100 um DRAM micro-tiles onto panels
idea: Borrow microLED mass transfer: release 100 um DRAM micro-tiles from the wafer by undercut etch and pick 10,000 at once with elastomer stamps onto large panels carrying RDL and logic chiplets.
why: Panel-scale assembly cuts packaging cost per bit 3-5x and harvests good tiles from every wafer at near-100% (Fact 6).

title: Open-hardware process chambers built by U.S. machine shops
idea: Worse: depend on a handful of tool vendors with 18-month lead times. Flip: fund open-source reference designs for ALD, etch and furnace modules with standard SEMI interfaces and open controllers. A national lab qualifies each once; regional machine shops then build and service them, like certified aircraft parts.
why: Tool capex (~70-80% of fab cost): targets ~40-50% cheaper non-litho tools with ~6-month lead times and U.S. manufacturing.

title: Base-array mask ROM with one e-beam-written via layer
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: pre-build generic NOR-ROM wafers (4F2 transistor arrays, DUV plus SAQP, ~25 masks, no capacitor) in bulk; once a model is frozen, program its weights by e-beam direct-writing a single via layer with two via sizes per bit-pair (2 bits/cell), so inference weights live in silicon with zero refresh and zero standby.
why: Weights are most of inference memory; ROM cost per bit could be ~3-5x below DRAM (no HAR capacitors, no EUV, ~40% fewer masks), frees DRAM for KV and activations, and maskless customization avoids per-model mask sets (facts 3, 4).

title: 3D XPoint rebuilt vertically: one hole mask for 200 layers
idea: 3D XPoint died on cost: every deck needed its own critical patterning and tall double etch, so two decks never undercut DRAM enough. Use the 3D NAND recipe instead: stack 200 metal/oxide word planes, drill one hole array, line holes with a self-selecting chalcogenide film and fill with a metal bitline pillar, so every plane-pillar crossing is a cell made with the same single critical mask.
why: Meets 100x: litho amortized over 200 layers like NAND, est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: ~1e8-1e9 endurance (wear-leveled behind a small DRAM cache), us-class writes, thermal disturb between planes.

title: Black-silicon MacEtch: catalytic wet etching of 100:1 capacitor holes
idea: Borrowed from solar black-silicon texturing, where Ag/Au catalyst sinks into silicon in HF/H2O2 and drills vertical pores: deposit an amorphous-Si capacitor mold, pattern a thin gold mesh on the hole lattice, immerse so the catalyst etches straight down to AR >100 at room temperature, strip the gold and line with electrode and dielectric; a small team runs it on a wet bench.
why: Facts 1/4: replaces a $10M+ high-AR plasma etcher with a ~$100k wet bench and has no aspect-ratio-dependent slowdown; gold contamination and verticality control are risks.

title: Catalytic gold-mesh wet etching drills 200:1 nanoholes
idea: Inverts 'deep holes require plasma'. Metal-assisted chemical etching: a perforated Au film (stepper-defined then spacer-shrunk) sinks into Si in HF/H2O2, drilling straight pores or freeing pillars at AR 100-200:1 at room temperature, then the Au is stripped in iodide before any thermal step.
why: Replaces the most expensive high-AR dry etchers (facts 1, 4) with wet benches, with no bowing; serves capacitor holes or vertical-channel pillars.

title: Metal-assisted wet etching carves 150:1 buried trench capacitors
idea: Constraint: no high-AR plasma etcher in the fab. A patterned Pt catalyst mesh sinks into single-crystal silicon in HF/H2O2 (MacEtch), carving 150:1 trenches at room temperature on a wet bench; the catalyst is stripped and reclaimed and the trenches become buried capacitors under the access transistors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR 150 in crystalline silicon gives ~10 fF cells; a ~$2M wet bench replaces an $8-10M etcher; the top surface is freed for wiring.

title: Wafer-scale capacitorless memory bonded face-to-face onto compute wafers
idea: Ideal: memory with no package, dicing or interposer. Closest: a full 300 mm wafer of logic-process gain-cell memory is hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer onto a wafer-scale accelerator; defective memory tiles are routed around by the compute wafer's network and test happens once per wafer pair.
why: Facts 5 and 6: removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x area/bit) and interposer/packaging capex; data movement <0.5 pJ/bit; yield loss handled by architecture.

title: Vicinal-wafer atomic step bunches as litho-free wordline templates
idea: First principle: a Si wafer miscut by angle theta has atomic steps every a/tan(theta), and controlled step bunching during anneal forms periodic facets at a 10-30 nm pitch set only by theta and temperature. Decorate the bunched step edges by step-flow selective deposition (e.g., CaF2 or a silicide) to make parallel hard-mask lines across the whole wafer in one anneal, with zero lithography, for the wordline and bitline layers.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): line/space layers made with no mask and no scanner; pitch comes from crystallography instead of optics.

title: Bicycle gears: one ferroelectric capacitor shifts between DRAM mode and NV mode
idea: Random stimulus 'bicycle gears' -> a near-antiferroelectric HZO cell runs as a fast linear high-k (k~40) DRAM capacitor during operation, with unlimited endurance because the polarization does not switch. On a power-fail signal, a plate-line pulse shifts every row into remanent polarization, so the polarization flips only at power events.
why: Non-volatile when it matters and unlimited endurance in normal use. One capacitor module replaces separate DRAM plus NVDIMM/flash backup, and high k eases the charge wall (fact 1).

title: Sourdough starter: bacterial S-layer protein crystals as nanohole templates
idea: Random stimulus 'sourdough starter' (living culture self-propagates) -> recrystallized bacterial surface-layer proteins form 2D lattices with 10-30 nm spacing and hexagonal or square symmetry on wafers. They are used, after mineralization, as hardmask templates for storage-node hole arrays, and their crystallization is guided by a coarse prepattern.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): the protein is grown in fermenters for cents per wafer and gives a sub-20 nm periodic template with no EUV.

title: Hard-drive head fabs make magnetic working memory
idea: Po: the disk-drive factory makes RAM. HDD read-head fabs already deposit and ion-mill sub-20 nm MTJ stacks at volume; as head demand flattens, use their deposition and milling lines to add SOT-MRAM layers onto 28 nm CMOS wafers shipped in from mature foundries, as a refresh-free DRAM-class tier.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: reuses existing MTJ capacity and skills instead of building MRAM fabs; no refresh, unlimited-class endurance with SOT.

title: Helium-free fab: hydrogen-neon chuck cooling and hydrogen-tracer leak checks
idea: Constraint: zero helium deliveries. Switch electrostatic-chuck backside cooling in high-AR etch and deposition from He to H2/Ne blends with redesigned micro-groove chucks that restore gas conductance, replace He leak testing with 5% H2/N2 tracer sniffers, and membrane-recapture any legacy He.
why: Removes exposure to the Qatar helium outage (~30% of supply) that can idle etch-heavy DRAM lines; mainly supply-risk removal, ~1-2% gas cost saving.

title: Jewelry lost-wax: sacrificial zinc-oxide layers for lateral 3D cavities
idea: Lost-wax casting relies on a filler that is easy to remove; build the 3D DRAM tier stack with sputtered ZnO sacrificial layers between Si or SiN tiers, then dissolve the ZnO in dilute acetic acid, which leaves Si, SiO2 and SiN untouched, carving micron-deep lateral capacitor cavities from one vertical slit.
why: 3D capacitor blocker (fact 2): replaces SiGe epitaxy and aggressive vapor etch with sputtering and a mild wet etch, cutting epi tool needs and recess variability; Zn and O are abundant.

title: Airport baggage CT: inline X-ray laminography for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Adapt CT and laminography from airport scanners and BGA inspection into an inline compact-source X-ray laminography tool that reconstructs tier-by-tier recess depth, channel thickness and capacitor fill in 100-tier 3D DRAM stacks on every lot without cross-sectioning.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) and ramp speed: replaces slow destructive TEM; cutting ramp by months is worth ~$1B on a $15B fab.

title: Area-selective ALD merges wordline-module patterning and deposition
idea: Combine area-selective ALD (inhibitor monolayers that block growth on SiN/SiO2) with the buried-wordline module. The gate dielectric grows only on exposed trench silicon and the Mo/TiN wordline grows only on that dielectric, so recess, cap and isolation self-align without block masks.
why: Cuts ~2 masks and ~15 dep/etch/clean steps in the wordline module, ~4% fewer tool-hours per wafer (fact 4).

title: Ion-irradiation defines spin-Hall MRAM bits magnetically without stack etching
idea: Effect: irradiation-induced interface intermixing plus the spin Hall effect. Deposit a blanket MTJ stack on a W or BiSb spin-Hall write line, then irradiate through a stencil with low-dose He+ or Ar+, which intermixes CoFeB/MgO and kills perpendicular anisotropy everywhere except the bits. Bits switch by spin-orbit torque from the in-plane spin Hall current, with no MTJ etch at all.
why: Capital and yield: MTJ ion-beam etch with redeposition is MRAM's yield and cost killer; a planar, etch-free flow saves ~3 masks and the IBE tools, making SOT working memory cheaper to build in the U.S.

title: Mo: subtractive dry-etched molybdenum metal layers with no CMP
idea: Deposit blanket Mo, pattern it with dry Cl2/O2 etch, then gap-fill with flowable dielectric cured by UV, the reverse of Cu/W damascene, so the metal layer needs no CMP and no post-CMP clean.
why: Water: deletes CMP and post-CMP scrub on each metal layer (>10x for the module); resources: removes tungsten (China ~80%).

title: Ion-implant isolation defines MRAM bits without etching the stack
idea: Ideal: magnetic bits with no etch of the magnetic stack. Closest: deposit a blanket perpendicular MTJ film and define cells with a masked light-ion plus oxygen implant that kills anisotropy and makes the inter-bit film resistive, leaving a planar, unetched stack with no redeposition or sidewall shorts.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: no capacitor or refresh; removes the MTJ ion-beam etch that limits MRAM pitch and yield, so pitch could shrink toward ~30 nm; 10^12+ endurance with VCMA writing.

title: Subtractively etched ruthenium wiring: no copper damascene, no barriers
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: deposit blanket Ru, plasma-etch it into lines and gap-fill with dielectric, skipping trench etch, barrier/seed, plating and Cu CMP; ruthenium's high melting point gives ~10x electromigration headroom at 125 C and nothing can diffuse into the cells.
why: Facet: drops ~4 tool types per metal level (plating, barrier PVD, Cu CMP, anneal); interconnect cost -20% with long-life EM margin.

title: Arrhenius rebinning sells retention-reject DRAM into temperature-guaranteed liquid-cooled racks
idea: Effect: thermally activated (Arrhenius) junction leakage, with retention roughly doubling every ~10 C cooler. Buy retention-downgraded DRAM parts at scrap prices, screen them on a ~$250k rig at 45 C and 64 ms refresh, and ship them only on liquid-cooled CXL memory modules whose controller firmware enforces a hard 50 C ceiling and throttles above it. $1M covers the rig, firmware and qualification within 24 months.
why: Raises usable supply with zero fab capital: if even 1-2% of world output is downbinned for retention, recovering it equals the output of part of a multi-billion-dollar fab.

title: DRAM wafer-start futures market lets AI labs pre-fund fabs
idea: Extreme user: AI labs whose memory demand swings 4x in a year. Create a standardized exchange-traded contract for 'wafer starts in year+3', so buyers lock capacity and fab builders raise construction capital against sold futures instead of balance sheets.
why: Capital intensity: shifts ~30-50% of fab financing risk to buyers who value certainty; smooths boom-bust and speeds new capacity.

title: Carbon-fiber furnaces: iron-catalyzed nanotube forests as capacitor cores
idea: Adapt carbon-fiber and nanotube-forest CVD: place Fe catalyst dots on Al2O3 at each storage-node pad, grow vertical multiwall carbon nanotubes 1-2 um tall at ~450-550 C, then ALD-wrap them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN so each tube is the scaffold and conductor of a tall capacitor that is grown rather than etched.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and etch capex (fact 4): AR >100 comes free with growth, removing the mold, hardmask and deep-etch module; Fe, C, Al, Ti, Zr, N only.

title: Cleanroom-free fab: sealed wafer mini-environments in plain warehouse
idea: Po: the fab has no cleanroom. Keep every wafer in nitrogen-purged sealed pods and tool-integrated ISO-1 mini-environments docking through gasketed ports, so the building is an ordinary ISO-8 warehouse into which modular tool pods are trucked and plugged.
why: Fab capital and time (fact 4): cleanroom shell, makeup air and subfab are ~25-35% of construction cost and 1-2 years of schedule; ~20-30% lower fab $ and faster time to output.

title: Molecular-ruler multilayers define 10 nm gaps between electrodes
idea: Box: oxide-node charge x lateral nanogap TFT x current sensing x 2D x Si x molecular-ruler lithography. Alternating phosphonate/metal-ion layers self-assemble on a parent electrode to a thickness counted in molecules (~1.5 nm per layer), a second metal is deposited and lifted off, and dissolving the ruler leaves a precise gap for a channel or dielectric.
why: Critical dimension from self-assembly count, not litho resolution (fact 4), with beakers, an evaporator and a contact aligner; risk is wafer-scale uniformity and ruler defects.

title: Twin landing pads let EUV expose at half dose
idea: Inverts 'one printed feature per electrical function'. Give every storage node two parallel, slightly offset contact/landing-pad features so a stochastic missing or bridged print of one is electrically harmless, then expose those stochastics-limited layers at ~50% EUV dose.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited; halving dose on 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers raises scanner wafers/hour ~40-60% (fact 4) for a few-to-10% cell-area cost.

title: Deep trench capacitors etched into the thinned wafer backside
idea: First principle: frontside capacitors compete for height inside a ~2 um back-end stack, while the substrate below the transistor is idle volume. After frontside transistors are made and bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer to ~1.5 um and etch single-crystal Si trenches (AR ~40, which etches more uniformly than oxide/nitride molds) from the backside, aligned to the storage nodes with backside-power-delivery alignment tools.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): decouples the capacitor from frontside wiring and reuses the BSPDN tooling now being installed for logic.

title: Substitute access transistors with BEOL two-terminal selectors in line-space crosspoints
idea: Build a 1S1C crosspoint: a threshold-switching selector (NbOx or OTS) in series with a planar MIM capacitor at each intersection of two perpendicular line arrays, which need only line/space patterning (SAQP or DSA, no contact holes, no EUV) and stack in BEOL; only the single selected intersection is charged or read.
why: Constraint: bit-granular access on short 4F2 lines gives ~0.2-0.5 pJ per useful bit versus 5.9 pJ (>=10x); facet: ~3 masks per layer, BEOL-stackable. Selector leakage forces frequent refresh.

title: H: hydrogen-blister peeling stacks tiers from one reusable donor
idea: Implant H into a donor Si wafer, bond to the target, split at the blister plane to transfer a 30-50 nm single-crystal tier, smooth by H2 anneal, then repeat 26+ times from the same donor with low-temperature device steps between transfers.
why: Fact 2: replaces long SiGe/Si epitaxial stacks with repeated layer transfer; tier quality equals bulk Si and one donor feeds many tiers.

title: Mask ROM's per-design killer fixed: imprinted ROM for frozen AI weights
idea: Mask ROM died because every code change needed new masks and weeks of lead time. Frozen AI model weights are read every token but almost never rewritten, so store them in 16-deck 3D diode-ROM where every layer is a common template except one via layer per model, imprinted from a template e-beam-cut in a day, with 2 bits/cell coded by via size.
why: Meets 100x: no capacitor, no refresh, a single custom layer; est. ~$0.01-0.05/GB with low read energy. Trade: immutable, so a new model needs new dies and KV-cache still uses DRAM.

title: Plated-wire memory reborn as thermally drawn crossbar ribbons
idea: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, 1960s-70s) died because hand-made wires could not reach semiconductor density. Thermally draw a preform of parallel metal electrodes embedded in a phase-change chalcogenide glass cladding down ~1000x into ribbons with ~200 nm electrode pitch, then laminate ribbons at 90 degrees so every electrode crossing becomes a cell, 50 laminations deep.
why: Meets 100x: patterning by a ~$5M drawing tower producing km per hour instead of lithography; est. ~$0.05/GB. Trades: coarse pitch, ribbon-registration yield, PCM endurance and write energy.

title: Let the pores place the cells: anodic alumina template
idea: Reverse 'cells define holes': anodize aluminum into a self-ordered hexagonal pore array (~40-60 nm pitch, AR >500), use the pores as capacitor molds, then self-align the access transistors to the pore lattice instead of drawing them by litho.
why: Capacitor charge wall: AR far above 75:1 without plasma etch or EUV; the main capacitor module litho goes away.

title: Bond a sense amp under every 64 cells; shrink capacitors
idea: Inverts 'bitlines must be long and capacitive'. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array at ~250 nm pitch so each local bitline serves only ~64 cells, cutting bitline capacitance from ~60 fF to ~8 fF; the cell then needs only ~1-1.5 fF, a stubby AR ~10:1 capacitor.
why: Breaks the charge wall (fact 1) by changing the transfer ratio, not the charge; removes the deepest etch, ~4 masks and much of the fill tool set.

title: Burn-in deleted; field scrubbing absorbs infant-mortality bits
idea: Combine the patrol-scrub engine with infant-mortality physics: DRAM ships without 125 C multi-hour burn-in, because early-life weak bits (well under 1% of cells) surface as correctable errors that the scrubber remaps in the first weeks of service.
why: Burn-in ovens, boards and floor space are a notable share of test capex and cycle time; removing them cuts back-end cost ~3-5% and cycle time 1-2 days.

title: Magnetotactic self-registration aligns HBM dies without precision bonders
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria align magnetosome chains to a field; electroplate a coded pattern of CoFe nanomagnet dots on each die backside and a matching soft-magnetic pattern on the target, float dies on a thin fluid film in a uniform field so they snap into <200 nm registration, then bond the whole batch in one anneal.
why: Replaces serial thermo-compression and hybrid bonders (~$3-5M each, ~1k units/hour) with batch self-assembly for HBM stacks (fact 6); est. 10x stacking throughput and ~80% less bonding capex.

title: Bond eight DRAM wafers before dicing: TSV-free wafer-stacked HBM
idea: Replace die-by-die microbump stacking with sequential wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding of 8-12 DRAM wafers, using fine-pitch bonded vias through 5 um-thinned silicon instead of large TSVs, then dice the finished stack once.
why: Cuts the HBM TSV area tax (Fact 6) by 2-3x and deletes per-die microbump and underfill steps; throughput scales per wafer, not per die.

title: Periphery from depreciated U.S. logic fabs, hybrid-bonded to array
idea: First principle: the array needs the finest pitch, but the periphery (~49% of the die) only needs ~28 nm-class CMOS. Make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab and the periphery on fully depreciated 28-65 nm U.S. logic fabs, then join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: up to ~1.8x bits per expensive DRAM wafer, using idle U.S. mature-node capacity.

title: Pastry chef's mille-feuille: slice deposited film stacks into line layers
idea: A pastry chef makes thin lines by slicing layered dough. Deposit ~10,000 alternating 6 nm conductor/dielectric films (thickness held to angstroms by ALD or sputter) on a carrier, saw the stack perpendicular to the layers into ribbons, polish them, and tile the ribbons face-down onto the array as a pre-made bitline or wordline layer whose pitch was set by film thickness, not lithography.
why: Turns the densest litho layers into a deposition-thickness problem with zero masks, giving sub-12 nm pitch without EUV. Speculative: ribbon tiling and alignment, polishing damage, and contact landing.

title: Bi: capillary-infiltrated molten Bi-Sn fills high-AR cavities
idea: Coat the array with a thin wetting liner, flood with molten Bi-Sn eutectic (~140 C) under gas pressure so it wicks into capacitor top-plate cavities and plugs, then wipe the excess with a heated blade before it freezes; Bi's solidification expansion offsets shrink voids.
why: Replaces slow CVD SiGe/W top-plate and plug fill with an atmospheric tool ~1/10 the cost, and removes tungsten (China ~80%) from those layers.

title: Bosch-etched TSVs and deep-trench storage cells in one etch
idea: Combine MEMS Bosch deep-reactive-ion etching with eDRAM-style deep-trench capacitors on 200 mm MEMS/power fabs. One DRIE step cuts both the stack TSVs and 40 um-deep trench capacitors (Cs >100 fF) for a relaxed-pitch, near-refresh-free buffer DRAM die.
why: Uses abundant, depreciated U.S. 200 mm capacity. Huge Cs cuts refresh ~100x (fact 3), and the TSV step becomes a shared step rather than an added tax (fact 6). Density is low, so this is a buffer/cache tier.

title: Si: plasma dicing and dry thinning for HBM die
idea: Finish thinning HBM DRAM wafers with high-rate SF6 plasma instead of wet polishing, and singulate with deep reactive-ion plasma dicing instead of water-cooled blade sawing; die edges come out chip-free.
why: Fact 6 (HBM yield -20-30%): chipping and microcracks fall; grinding/sawing water and slurry for the module fall >10x.

title: Substitute tungsten wordlines and contacts with chlorine-ALD molybdenum
idea: Replace WF6-based tungsten in buried wordlines, bitline contacts and periphery plugs with molybdenum deposited by ALD from MoO2Cl2, eliminating the TiN barrier and nucleation layers that fluorine chemistry demands. Mo's shorter electron mean free path gives lower resistivity than W below ~15 nm line width.
why: Scarce resource (China ~80% of W) and U.S. supply (Colorado Mo mines); 20-40% lower wordline resistance permits longer wordlines and fewer drivers, shrinking periphery (fact 7).

title: Swift heavy-ion latent tracks etch 200:1 capacitor holes in one wet step
idea: Effect: latent-track etching. A thick SiO2 or polymer mold is exposed to MeV-GeV heavy ions through a stencil with one aperture per cell; each ion leaves a damaged track that etches ~1000x faster than bulk in dilute HF, so every hole etches straight to AR 200:1 at once. Several tracks per aperture merge into one hole.
why: Fact 1: the AR ~115 needed for more charge is beyond plasma etch; a cyclotron beamline (already used roll-to-roll for track-etched membranes) replaces fleets of $10M+ cryo HAR etchers. A 40 nm-pitch stencil is the main risk.

title: Cross-company tool-hour exchange routes DRAM steps to idle tools
idea: Po: one fab has two owners. A secure scheduling exchange lets DRAM makers route non-critical steps (implant, CMP, anneal, ALD) to idle, contamination-qualified tools in nearby mature logic fabs via sealed-pod transfer, trading tool-hours like electricity.
why: Capital utilization: mature fabs often run ~70-80% utilized; borrowing hours relieves DRAM bottleneck tools ~10-15% without buying tools.

title: Fusion-bond stacks of sixteen thinned 180 nm array layers
idea: Inverts 'one wafer makes one memory layer'. Build cheap 180 nm array layers on 200 mm SOI, then oxide-fusion-bond and etch back 16 of them (the 1990s BESOI technique), connected by 2 um through-oxide vias at mat edges to a single bottom periphery layer.
why: ~16x density per footprint with no litho shrink; each layer costs depreciated-tool prices (facts 2, 4).

title: Eliminate the high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch with anodized alumina pores
idea: Deposit 2-3 um of aluminium over the landing pads, pre-dimple it with a shallow DUV-defined seed lattice, and anodize it so self-ordered hexagonal nanopores grow straight down onto each pad; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN then lines the pores. No resist, no hard mask and no HAR plasma etch are used for the storage node.
why: Facts 1 and 4: electrochemical pores reach AR >150:1 in a wet bath, enabling Cs ~8 fF, and remove the slowest, costliest etch module and its hard-mask stack; capacitor-module capex down an estimated ~40%.

title: Low-aspect-ratio capacitor from ALD rutile-TiO2/SrTiO3 on Ru, k~100
idea: Box: k 100-150 dielectric charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x ALD on Ru/RuO2 electrodes that template rutile or perovskite growth below 450 C. With k~100 vs ~40 today, the same ~5 fF fits in an AR ~25 pillar, so the module drops the cryo-etch, the support mesh and two hardmask layers; leakage is held by Al doping and a thin wide-gap interface layer.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) attacked through process: AR 70 to 25 removes the hardest etch and its helium-cooled tools, ~5-8% wafer cost; risk is leakage of narrow-gap high-k at ~0.4 nm EOT.

title: Open DRAM PDK portable across any 28-65 nm foundry
idea: Po: DRAM is open source. Publish an open, foundry-portable gain-cell/1T1C memory process design kit using only steps every 28-65 nm logic fab already runs (MIM capacitors, standard high-k, existing implants), so dozens of mature fabs can fill idle capacity with interchangeable memory dies.
why: Supply concentration and idle capacity: converts surplus mature wafer starts into multi-source memory with zero new fab.

title: Substitute separate memory die with DRAM built in logic wafer backside
idea: After the backside-power-delivery thinning step that 2 nm-class logic already performs, deposit an oxide-TFT plus MIM-capacitor array in the backside dielectric under the compute tiles, wired through the nano-TSVs the BSPDN flow already etches.
why: Constraint: 1-5 um vertical distance gives ~0.05-0.2 pJ/bit, >20x below HBM; capital: rides on a process step the logic fab already pays for, with no memory fab, package or TSV stack.

title: Substitute 77 K with 4 K quantum-paraelectric SrTiO3 planar capacitors
idea: Beside quantum computers and cryogenic accelerators, exploit SrTiO3's dielectric constant rising to ~10^4 at 4 K to make planar (AR ~1) 5 fF capacitors, with superconducting NbN bitlines and 0.2 V cryo-CMOS sensing.
why: Constraint: 0.2 V swing on lossless lines gives >=25x lower switching energy per access; facet: no HAR etch, no EUV. 4 K cooling overhead (~500-1000 W/W) means it fits only where 4 K already exists.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling with palladium recovery replaces scarce helium
idea: Ideal: etch and deposition need no helium. Closest: switch electrostatic-chuck backside gas to H2 (thermal conductivity close to He) at sub-flammable volumes, with a Pd-membrane capture-and-reuse loop on each tool; keep He only where H2 chemistry is incompatible.
why: Resource chokepoint (Qatar helium offline): DRAM etch/deposition are heavy He users; cuts He demand ~70-90%.

title: Depreciation arbitrage: keep paid-off 1y/1z DRAM lines running
idea: Po: the oldest fab makes the cheapest bit. Instead of converting fully depreciated 1y/1z-class DRAM lines to HBM, sign 5-year take-or-pay contracts for DDR4/LPDDR4/DDR5 at cash cost, steering auto, PC and edge demand there and freeing leading lines for AI.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4): paid-off lines run ~40-50% cheaper per wafer, offsetting ~1.5x lower density for near-parity cost per bit at zero capex.

title: Spare-tier HBM: thirteen dies for twelve, fused at test
idea: First principle: with die yield y = 0.98, a 12-high stack yields 0.98^12 = ~79%, but one spare die plus a TSV crossbar remap programmed by e-fuse after stack test gives P(at most 1 failure in 13) = ~97%. Add one redundant die per stack and steer around any bad die at test, and again in the field.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): 21% stack loss becomes ~3% for 8% extra silicon; repairable by design.

title: Accept 16 ms retention to delete recessed-channel process steps
idea: Time-shift the refresh interval from 64 ms to 16 ms and let a smart controller absorb the extra refreshes on a capacity-tier product; the looser leakage target lets a shallow-recess planar access transistor replace the buried saddle-fin, deleting the recess etch, halo implants and their masks.
why: Removes ~6-10 process steps and 2-3 implant masks (Facts 3, 4) for ~5-8% lower wafer cost, trading some refresh energy on low-activity memory.

title: Eliminate backgrinding waste: laser subsurface slicing of HBM core wafers
idea: Before TSV reveal, focus an infrared laser through the wafer back side to write a cleave plane ~40 um below the devices (as laser slicing does for SiC), split the device layer onto its carrier, and repolish the remaining ~700 um slab for reuse as monitor wafers or epitaxial donors. Resulting stacks are standard HBM.
why: HBM grinds away ~94% of each core wafer; reclaiming it cuts virgin-wafer demand (and Czochralski/crucible use) and removes grinding and CMP passes.

title: Wafer-level burn-in revived as contactless, self-powered on-wafer BIST
idea: Early wafer-level burn-in for DRAM failed on the cost and planarity of full-wafer probe contactors. Build a scribe-line power grid fed by two large pads per wafer; every die runs on-chip BIST and burn-in in a heated cassette, burns results into fuses and reports through an on-die photodiode/LED or near-field link.
why: Throughput and capex: removes probe cards and most ATE time from memory test, a large share of back-end capital; claims ~50-70% test-capex cut.

title: Conducting domain-wall memory in lithium-niobate-on-insulator wafers
idea: TRIZ #32 Changing properties: in thin-film LiNbO3 (made by smart-cut for photonic modulators) a voltage pulse writes a nanodomain whose inclined wall conducts while the bulk insulates; reading measures wall current non-destructively and the domain persists without power.
why: Zero refresh and non-destructive read (no restore energy, cf. fact 8); a planar two-electrode cell patterned by DUV in a dedicated back end reuses the LNOI photonics supply chain, with 1e10-class endurance reported (facts 3, 4).

title: Substitute passive silicon interposer with DRAM-filled active interposer under GPU
idea: The ~2,500 mm2 CoWoS interposer is mostly empty 65 nm-class silicon; build deep-trench-capacitor eDRAM arrays into it (deep trenches are already etched there for decoupling caps) so the GPU's hot working set sits ~50 um below the logic through hybrid bonds instead of across an HBM PHY.
why: Constraint: vertical access ~0.2-0.4 pJ/bit versus HBM 3-4 pJ/bit (>=10x); capital: reuses interposer wafer starts and trench tools already in the packaging flow, adding a few GB without TSV stacks.

title: Battery chemist: room-temperature electrochemical ALD electrodes in capacitor holes
idea: A battery chemist grows metal one atomic layer at a time. Use electrochemical ALD: deposit an underpotential monolayer (Cu or Pb), galvanically swap it for Pt or Ru, and repeat, so electrodes grow conformally in 200:1 capacitor holes from aqueous solution at room temperature.
why: Gives conformal electrodes without vacuum ALD chambers (~$4M vs ~$0.5M electrochemical cell), enabling deeper capacitors at lower capex. High risk: minutes per nm, and uneven potential deep in holes.

title: Two bits per cell in trailing fabs with fat capacitors
idea: Po: one cell remembers two things. Old 2x-3x nm DRAM lines have larger capacitors and tighter leakage tails; store four charge levels per cell and read with reference-cell-calibrated time-to-digital sense amps (built in bonded 28 nm periphery), doubling bits on existing lines.
why: Density on existing capacity: ~1.8x bits per wafer of an old line, closing much of its gap to 1b nodes without new tools.

title: Shipyard block construction: prefabricated fab modules built in parallel
idea: Shipyards build fully outfitted hull blocks in parallel halls and join them at the dock; build a DRAM fab as ~300 factory-made blocks (subfab utility skids, pre-piped tool pads, ceiling cassettes with fan filters, abatement modules) made off-site in a U.S. yard while foundations are poured, then craned in and bolted together.
why: Time-to-capacity and capital (fact 4): build time 3-5 years toward ~18-24 months, cutting capitalized interest; repeated block designs give a learning curve across multiple U.S. fabs.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as 100:1 capacitor molds on chip
idea: Box: MIM charge x sputtered IGZO TFT x voltage sense amp x BEOL test chip x Si/SiO2 x two-step Al anodization in oxalic acid. A sputtered Al film is anodized into hexagonally ordered pores (~60-100 nm pitch, AR >100) with positions seeded by a light EBL pre-pattern, then ALD TiN/HfO2/TiN coats the pores, so the capacitor mold forms in a beaker, not a cryo-etcher.
why: Capacitor module capital (fact 1): a ~$2k anodization bath replaces a $5M+ high-AR etcher, with AR 100-500 possible (10-30 fF/cell); every step uses university sputter, EBL, ALD and wet benches.

title: Shift burn-in from oven hours to fleet weeks
idea: Time-shift the reliability screen: skip factory burn-in ovens and long retention tests, ship dies with on-die BIST that runs adaptive stress patterns during the first weeks of server idle time, and retire weak rows through the host before data is trusted.
why: Burn-in and test are ~10% of DRAM cost and heavy capital; cutting them ~70% saves ~5-7% per bit and frees tester capacity.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in etch and deposition chucks
idea: First principle: helium is used under wafers only for heat transfer (0.15 W/m-K), and H2 conducts heat better (0.18 W/m-K) and can be made from water anywhere. Re-engineer electrostatic chucks to run 5-15 Torr pure-H2 backside gas with millimole-scale inventory, hydrogen sensors and catalytic recombiners on the chamber exhaust.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline since March 2026): removes one of the largest fab uses of helium and protects uptime from price spikes.

title: Photo-patternable metal-oxo films become the cell dielectric, no etch
idea: Extreme user: $1 printed-electronics IoT, where photo-curable sol-gel oxides are routine. Spin a Hf/Zr oxo-cluster film with carboxylate ligands, expose it so exposed areas crosslink, develop in a non-fluorinated solvent and anneal it into the final high-k dielectric: no resist, no PAG, no etch.
why: Process steps: collapses coat/expose/etch/strip into coat/expose/develop for dielectric layers (~4 fewer steps per layer) and removes PFAS photoacid generators.

title: Self-calibrating sense amplifiers let periphery use relaxed transistors
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: each sense amp stores its own offset on its bitline capacitance during a pre-sense calibration phase, and a per-mat trim register is updated at power-up, raising tolerable Vt mismatch from ~10 mV to ~40 mV.
why: Lets periphery use cheaper, higher-variation transistors (fewer halo/Vt implant masks, mature-node periphery wafers) and shrinks SA area (fact 7, capital).
